title: National Health Amendment (Simplified Price Disclosure) Bill 2013
short_title: National Health Amendment (Simplified Price Disclosure) Bill 2013

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would simplify how the government adjusts drug prices under the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme.
It would merge all medicines into a single price disclosure cycle and shorten each cycle from 18 months to 12 months.
The first price reduction under the changes would occur on 1 October 2014, with a test requiring the market price to be at least 10% below the PBS price before a reduction applies.
changes: The bill merges all medicines into one ongoing price disclosure cycle.
It shortens each price disclosure cycle from 18 months to 12 months.
It applies a test requiring the market price to be at least 10% below the PBS price before a reduction takes effect.
summary.affected: The government, consumers, and drug companies supplying medicines under the PBS and RPBS.

speeches.speaker: Peter Dutton
speeches.brief: Moved that the bill be read a second time, stating that simplified PBS price disclosure will merge three cycles into one, reduce each cycle from 18 months to 12 months, and produce savings of $835 million commencing 1 October 2014 while bringing subsidised medicine prices closer to market prices.

speeches.speaker: Catherine King
speeches.brief: Supported the National Health Amendment (Simplified Price Disclosure) Bill 2013 but moved a second reading amendment demanding the projected $835 million in savings be reinvested in health, noting the PBS caps concession patient costs at $5.90 per medicine and highlighted delayed listing of the cystic fibrosis drug Kalydeco.

speeches.speaker: Bert Van Manen
speeches.brief: Supported the National Health Amendment (Simplified Price Disclosure) Bill 2013, describing how the reform will shorten price disclosure cycles from 18 to 12 months to deliver an estimated $835 million in savings, but raised concerns that community pharmacists have seen rents rise by 40 per cent with no compensation for expired stock.

speeches.speaker: Pat Conroy
speeches.brief: Supported the bill and Labor's amendment requiring savings to stay in health, noted bulk-billing reached 82 per cent under Labor compared with 67 per cent when the current Prime Minister was health minister, and criticised the government's abolition of the Alcohol and Other Drugs Council after nearly 50 years of operation.

speeches.speaker: Jill Hall
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, recalling Labor's National Health Reform Agreement to invest $20 billion in hospitals over 10 years, and noted bulk-billing rates in her Shortland electorate rose above 80 per cent under Labor compared with under 60 per cent during the Howard years.

speeches.speaker: Amanda Rishworth
speeches.brief: Moved a second reading amendment requiring the bill's projected $830 million in savings over four years to be reinvested in health, noting Labor previously invested $1.9 billion from earlier price disclosure savings into projects like integrated cancer centres, and condemned the $100 million cut to the Royal Victorian Eye and Ear Hospital.

speeches.speaker: Peter Dutton
speeches.brief: Rejected Labor's second reading amendment as a political stunt while defending the National Health Amendment (Simplified Price Disclosure) Bill 2013 as necessary to keep the PBS sustainable, and said the government would consult with industry differently than the previous government had before implementing the changes.

acts.title: National Health Amendment (Simplified Price Disclosure) Act 2014
